title: Two-phonon pairing and superconductivity in $SrTiO_3$
authors: Antonio Santacesaria, Cristiano Muzzi, Maria Eleonora Temperini, Paolo Barone, Maria N. Gastiasoro, José Lorenzana
abstract: We explore the possibility that the two-phonon pairing mechanism proposed by Ngai can explain superconductivity in doped strontium titanate (STO). The two-phonon deformation potential is evaluated using two distinct theoretical estimates based on first-principles calculations and two empirical estimates based on experimental data, yielding very large values of the same order of magnitude. We derive the effective electron-electron interaction mediated by two-phonon exchange. Crucial to our computations is the strong dispersion of the involved soft phonons. Because the scale of the two-phonon interaction is much larger than the Fermi energy, the Migdal theorem does not apply. We obtain a one-loop Eliashberg equation that can be solved in the weak-coupling limit. We find that despite the significant electron-phonon matrix element, phase space considerations considerably reduce the effective coupling. A two-phonon mechanism can not be excluded based on the $T_c$ magnitude, but its value is dominated by the high-energy-frequency physics and is weakly affected by the soft-phonon behavior. The theory predicts a $T_c$ that monotonously increases with doping, which is not in accordance with the experiment. We identify the conditions for a two-phonon mechanism to be effective in other materials and discuss possible candidates.
summary: This work theoretically explores if two-phonon interactions can explain superconductivity in doped strontium titanate. Using advanced calculations derived from DFT, the authors solve an Eliashberg equation to predict $T_c$. The key finding is that while the mechanism is plausible, the theoretical prediction for doping dependence contradicts experimental results.
main_problem: The study investigates whether a two-phonon pairing mechanism, proposed by Ngai, can account for superconductivity observed in doped strontium titanate (STO).
main_result: While the theory predicts a superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) that increases monotonically with doping, this contradicts experimental observations. The coupling strength is found to be dominated by high-energy physics.
method: The authors derive an effective electron-electron interaction mediated by two-phonon exchange and solve a one-loop Eliashberg equation in the weak-coupling limit.
model_or_system: The system is doped strontium titanate ($	ext{SrTiO}_3$), modeled using coupled electronic and lattice Hamiltonians. The analysis incorporates the electron-two-phonon interaction term, $\mathcal{H}_{	ext{el}-2	ext{ph}}$, which is crucial for determining pairing.
key_observables: Superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$) as a function of doping; effective coupling constant ($\lambda$).
important_parameters: The two-phonon deformation potential coefficient ($\alpha$); the Fermi energy scale relative to phonon frequencies (where Migdal theorem fails).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the soft mode is well-represented by the Slater mode and neglects variations in band mass. The applicability of the Eliashberg theory is confirmed despite strong coupling terms.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the $	ext{SrTiO}_3$ unit cell and Slater mode displacements, while Figure 2 illustrates how electronic bands are affected by frozen phonon displacements.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework using DFT calculations to estimate the two-phonon coupling strength ($\alpha$) via multiple methods (DFT shifts, total energy fitting, empirical data). It then applies this interaction within a one-loop Eliashberg theory to predict $T_c$ versus doping.
why_interesting: Although focused on phonon-mediated superconductivity, the theoretical framework involves solving complex many-body equations (Eliashberg) and analyzing strong coupling limits, which shares mathematical structure with models used in strongly correlated systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1. SrTiO3 cubic unit cell. We show oxygen atoms in red, titanium atoms in blue, and strontium atoms in green. Black arrows represent the Slater mode displacements, for which oxygen atoms move coherently as a cage with opposite phases with respect to the titanium atom while strontium atoms are fixed in their equilibrium position. Notice that DFT calculations have been made with the tetragonal unit cell.

Figure 2. Equilibrium doubly degenerate bands (black) and band structure in the presence of a Slater frozen phonon (1 blue, 2 red and 3 green). Directions are indexed in pseudocubic coordinates. The lattice displacement is along [010] with magnitude uS = 0.02 ˚A. Notice that this displacement is much smaller than the estimated zero-point motion of the soft mode (ls ≈0.3 ˚A). The small splitting of each band at finite wave-vector along [100] is due to the Rashba mechanism, while the rigid shift at Γ can be attributed to the two-phonon mechanism.

Figure 3. Band shift δn as a function of the relative displace- ment between oxygen and titanium squared u2 S. Solid symbols are the DFT data, while the lines are a linear fit. The dif- ferent colors indicate the three lower bands using the same conventions as Fig. 2 (band 1: blue, 2: red, and 3: green). Triangles and solid lines refer to computations for uS along the c-direction, while circles and dashed lines are taken for uS along (010) in pseudocubic coordinates (a+b in the tetragonal ones), which corresponds nearly to the Ti-O-Ti bond direction in the basal plane.

Figure 4. Total DFT energy as a function of the displacement in the Slater mode polarized along the tetragonal aT axis (pseu- docubic [110] direction) for different band fillings n. Points are fitted using a quartic function E(u) = Ku2/2 + V4u4, shown as a continuous line. The inset shows the effective stiffness constant as a function of band filling.

Figure 5. Linear (a) and quadratic (b) Holstein models. An electronic level with single particle energy ϵ interacts with a harmonic oscillator representing an ion. Blue arrows represent the electrons. In (a), the distance of the ion to the electronic site varies linearly with the displacement, while in (b), it varies quadratically. Assuming that the energy of the electronic level is linear in the distance leads to the linear and quadratic models. Comparing the energy of two electrons in the same sites (left panels) with the one of two electrons in different sites (right) allows us to obtain the attractive interaction.
